# Plan: Build and evaluate the triage agent with the SPE loop

## Core point
The spec says "triage tickets correctly and cheaply." That is too vague to test. Step 1 turns it into numbers. This plan is Prediction 001. It makes claims that the evals can prove wrong. After you approve, the eval workflow builds the agent, runs it, and scores each claim as pass or fail.

Nothing exists yet, so I chose Python and the Anthropic SDK as defaults. Tell me if you want a different stack.

## Gates
- I commit locally after each step. I do not push.
- I add no Co-Authored-By line and no Claude mention to commits.
- I touch no real ticket system. Jira and any helpdesk stay read-only and unused.
- Eval API spend is capped at $5 total. I stop and ask if a run would go over the cap.

## Step 1. Sharpen the spec
I will write `spe/spec.md`. It replaces the one-line prompt with testable criteria. These are my proposed defaults. Please correct them.

| Field | Default |
|---|---|
| Input | One ticket with a subject and a body in plain text |
| Output | JSON with `category`, `priority`, `team`, and a one-line `reason` |
| Categories | bug, feature_request, billing, account_access, how_to, spam |
| Priority | P1 (outage or data loss), P2, P3, P4 |
| Teams | engineering, billing, support, none (for spam) |
| "Correctly" | Category accuracy of at least 90%. P1 recall of at least 95%. Valid JSON on 100% of tickets. |
| "Cheaply" | Mean cost per ticket under $0.001. p95 latency under 3 seconds. |

P1 recall gets its own bar because a missed outage is the most costly error. A P3 ticket labeled P4 costs little.

Commit: `spe: add sharpened triage spec`

## Step 2. Record Prediction 001
I will write `spe/predictions/001.md`. Each claim says what I expect, why, and how sure I am.

| ID | Prediction | Confidence |
|---|---|---|
| P1 | One prompt on a small, low-cost model reaches 90% category accuracy or higher. | Medium |
| P2 | Priority accuracy is lower than category accuracy, at about 80%. Priority is more subjective. | Medium |
| P3 | P1 recall reaches 95% only after the prompt lists explicit outage signals. | Low |
| P4 | Most category errors fall between billing and account_access. | Medium |
| P5 | Mean cost per ticket stays under $0.001 when the system prompt is cached. | Medium |
| P6 | A larger model gains 5 points of accuracy or less, at 5 times the cost or more. The small model is the better choice. | Low |

I will look up current model IDs and prices in the Anthropic docs before I build. I will not trust memory for prices. I will list candidate models in this file and wait for you to approve the list.

Commit: `spe: record prediction 001`

## Step 3. Build the eval dataset
I will create `spe/evals/dataset/tickets.jsonl` with 120 labeled tickets.
- There are 20 tickets per category.
- At least 15 tickets are P1.
- 20 tickets are hard cases, such as a billing complaint that is really a login failure.
- I split the set into 80 dev tickets and 40 held-out tickets. I tune only on dev.

The tickets are synthetic because no real tickets exist yet. A model that writes and labels its own test set can grade itself too kindly. To reduce that risk, I will ask you to check 20 labels I pick at random. Real tickets from you would replace or add to this set.

Commit: `spe: add labeled ticket dataset`

## Step 4. Build the agent
- `triage/prompt.md` holds the system prompt with the category, priority, and team rules.
- `triage/agent.py` holds one function, `triage(ticket) -> dict`. It calls the model, checks the JSON against a schema, and retries once if the JSON is invalid.
- The function also returns input tokens, output tokens, and latency for cost tracking.

Commit: `triage: add first agent and prompt`

## Step 5. Build the graders and runner
- `spe/evals/graders.py` holds code-based graders only. They check category exact match, priority exact match, P1 recall, JSON validity, cost from token counts, and latency.
- I will not use an LLM judge in this round. Every score is deterministic and costs nothing to compute.
- `spe/evals/run.py` runs one model on one split. It writes `spe/results/<run-id>/scores.json` and `errors.jsonl`.

Commit: `spe: add graders and eval runner`

## Step 6. Run the eval workflow (after approval)
This workflow runs in this order.
1. Run each approved candidate model on the dev split.
2. Write a confusion matrix for category and for priority.
3. Score each prediction from P1 to P6 as pass, fail, or unclear. Each score cites the number it rests on.
4. Write `spe/results/run-001/verdict.md`.
5. If a prediction fails, I write `spe/predictions/002.md` with a new claim and one change to try. Then I rerun on dev.
6. I stop after 3 rounds or when the spec is met on dev, whichever comes first.
7. I run the chosen setup once on the held-out split. That number is the one I report.

Commit after each round: `spe: eval round N results and verdict`

## Step 7. Log
`spe/log.md` gets one entry per round. Each entry names the prediction, the result, and the change made next.

Commit: `spe: update loop log`

## Folder layout
```
spe/
  spec.md
  log.md
  predictions/001.md
  evals/dataset/tickets.jsonl
  evals/graders.py
  evals/run.py
  results/run-001/
triage/
  prompt.md
  agent.py
```

## Questions before I start
1. Are the categories, priorities, and teams in Step 1 right for your tickets?
2. Can you share 50 or more real tickets, with personal data removed?
3. Is $0.001 per ticket the right cost bar, and is $5 the right total eval budget?
4. Which models may I test? I will propose a list from current docs, but I need your approval before I run them.
critiques: Step 1 turns "correctly and cheaply" into numeric bars: category accuracy of at least 90%, P1 recall of at least 95%, valid JSON on 100% of tickets, cost under $0.001 per ticket, and p95 latency under 3 seconds. Step 5 lists a code grader for each of these bars.

Most predictions carry numbers, such as "90% category accuracy or higher" and "about 80%". P4 has no number: "Most category errors fall between billing and account_access." The table is also not organized by configuration, because the candidate models are not named yet.

The plan says "Each claim says what I expect, why, and how sure I am," but the table has no Why column. Only P2 gives a reason ("Priority is more subjective"). P1, P5, and P6 give no reason for their numbers.
Step 2 writes and commits spe/predictions/001.md before any eval runs. The plan never saves a copy of itself to a file.
Step 6 goes straight to "Run each approved candidate model on the dev split." The plan has no grader selftest and no small dry run before the full run.

Step 5 lists graders for category, priority, P1 recall, JSON validity, cost, and latency. Step 6 adds confusion matrices. The plan never maps each prediction (P1 to P6) to a named grader, so the link is only implied, and P6 has no grader that compares model cost against model gain.

Step 6 scores each prediction as pass, fail, or unclear, with each score citing a number. It writes verdict.md and then writes predictions/002.md with a new claim when a prediction fails. Step 7 logs each round in spe/log.md.
